course.title: Differential Equations
course.description: How to write down and solve equations that describe change — first-order and second-order equations, modeling with them, oscillations and resonance, Laplace transforms, and a first look at systems and numerical methods. Structure adapted from MIT OpenCourseWare 18.03 Differential Equations (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) is an equation that relates an unknown function to…
options: the integral of a known function only
questions.explanation: An ODE ties a function to one or more of its derivatives, such as y' + y = 0 — see 'What an ODE is'.

questions.prompt: The general solution of dy/dx = k y is…
questions.explanation: Exponential growth or decay: the rate of change is proportional to the amount, giving y = C e^(k x).

questions.prompt: The integral of 1/x dx (for x > 0) is…
questions.explanation: The natural logarithm is the antiderivative of 1/x; you will need this in separable equations.

questions.prompt: Separating the variables in dy/dx = x y means rewriting it as…
questions.explanation: Collect all y with dy on one side and all x with dx on the other: dy/y = x dx.

questions.prompt: The characteristic equation of y'' - 5 y' + 6 y = 0 is…
questions.explanation: Replace y'' by r^2, y' by r, and y by 1 to get r^2 - 5 r + 6 = 0, whose roots are 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: The general solution of a second-order linear ODE contains how many arbitrary constants?
questions.explanation: The number of arbitrary constants matches the order of the equation, so a second-order equation has two.

questions.prompt: The derivative of e^(3 t) with respect to t is…
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, d/dt of e^(3 t) equals 3 e^(3 t).

questions.prompt: An initial condition such as y(0) = 5 is used to…
options: raise the order of the equation
questions.explanation: Initial conditions select one particular solution out of the whole family by fixing the constants.

lessons.title: What an ODE is, and reading a direction field
lessons.grammar_note: The order of an ODE is the highest derivative that appears: y' + y = 0 is first order, y'' + y = 0 is second order.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify an equation by its order, check whether a proposed function is a solution, and read a direction field to see how solutions flow — including where they hold steady. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, how many arbitrary constants should the general solution of a second-order equation have?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An ordinary differential equation relates an unknown function y(x) to its derivatives. A solution is any function that makes the equation true when substituted in. The order is the highest derivative present. A first-order equation can be written dy/dx = f(x, y). At every point (x, y) in the plane, f gives a slope; drawing a short line segment with that slope at many points produces a direction field (also called a slope field), and solution curves are the curves that stay tangent to those segments everywhere. When f depends on y alone, the equation is autonomous, and any value where f(y) = 0 gives a constant equilibrium solution — the solution just sits there. An equilibrium is stable if nearby solutions move toward it and unstable if they move away.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Check a solution: does y = e^(2 x) solve y' = 2 y? Its derivative is 2 e^(2 x), which equals 2 y, so yes. Order: y'' + 3 y' + 2 y = 0 has highest derivative y'', so it is second order. Direction field of dy/dx = y: above the x-axis (y > 0) slopes are positive, below it slopes are negative, and along y = 0 the slope is 0, so y = 0 is an equilibrium — an unstable one, since solutions run away from it. For dy/dx = -y the same line y = 0 is a stable equilibrium, since every nearby solution decays toward it. Logistic flow dy/dt = y (1 - y) has two equilibria, y = 0 (unstable) and y = 1 (stable).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the order of y''' + y' = x? 2) Verify that y = e^(-x) solves y' = -y. 3) For dy/dt = 2 y, is the equilibrium y = 0 stable or unstable? 4) Find every equilibrium of dy/dt = y (y - 3). 5) Along the line y = 1, what slope does the field dy/dx = x - y assign at the point (4, 1)? Answers: 1) third order. 2) y' = -e^(-x) = -y, so it works. 3) unstable, since solutions grow away from 0. 4) y = 0 and y = 3. 5) slope = 4 - 1 = 3.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the order (highest derivative) with the degree (the power on that derivative). Mistake: forgetting that a constant function can be a solution — equilibria are easy to miss. Exit: (a) What equation gives the slope in a first-order direction field? (b) What do you call a constant solution where f(y) = 0? Answers: dy/dx = f(x, y); an equilibrium solution.

lessons.title: First-order separable equations
lessons.grammar_note: Separable means dy/dx factors as g(x) h(y); once separated, integrate each side with respect to its own variable.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize when a first-order equation separates, split it into two single-variable integrals, and solve initial value problems — while spotting the constant solutions that separation can hide. Warm-up: how would you rewrite dy/dx = x y so that all the y terms sit with dy?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An equation is separable when dy/dx = g(x) h(y), a product of a function of x times a function of y. Move every y with dy to one side and every x with dx to the other: dy / h(y) = g(x) dx. Integrate both sides; each side is an ordinary single-variable integral. Add a single constant of integration (folding both into one C), then solve for y when you can. One caution: dividing by h(y) assumes h(y) is not zero, so any value where h(y) = 0 is a separate constant (equilibrium) solution that you must add back by hand.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Solve dy/dx = x y. Separate: dy/y = x dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x^2 / 2 + C, so y = A e^(x^2 / 2), where A = e^C is any nonzero constant; y = 0 is the extra constant solution. Solve dy/dx = -x / y. Separate: y dy = -x dx. Integrate: y^2 / 2 = -x^2 / 2 + C, i.e. x^2 + y^2 = R^2 — concentric circles. Initial value problem: dy/dx = y^2 with y(0) = 1. Separate: dy / y^2 = dx, so -1/y = x + C. At x = 0, y = 1 gives C = -1, hence y = 1 / (1 - x), which blows up as x approaches 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Separate dy/dx = 3 x^2 y. 2) Solve dy/dx = y with y(0) = 2. 3) Solve dy/dx = x / y. 4) What constant solution does dy/dx = y (1 - y) hide when you divide by y (1 - y)? 5) Solve dy/dt = -2 t y, y(0) = 5. Answers: 1) dy/y = 3 x^2 dx. 2) y = 2 e^x. 3) y dy = x dx, so y^2 - x^2 = C. 4) y = 0 and y = 1. 5) ln|y| = -t^2 + C, so y = 5 e^(-t^2).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: dividing by h(y) and silently dropping the solutions where h(y) = 0. Mistake: writing a separate constant on each side instead of a single combined C. Exit: (a) What form must dy/dx have to be separable? (b) After separating dy/dx = x y and integrating, what is the general solution? Answers: g(x) h(y); y = A e^(x^2 / 2), together with y = 0.

lessons.title: First-order linear equations and integrating factors
lessons.grammar_note: Standard form is y' + p(x) y = q(x); the coefficient of y' must be 1 before you compute the integrating factor.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Put a first-order linear equation in standard form, build its integrating factor, and solve it in one clean sweep. Warm-up: in y' + 2 y = 0, what is p(x)?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A first-order linear equation has the form y' + p(x) y = q(x): y and y' each appear to the first power and are not multiplied together. The trick is the integrating factor mu(x) = e^(integral of p(x) dx). Multiply the whole equation by mu. The left side then becomes exactly the derivative of the product mu y, because mu' = p mu; that is, (mu y)' = mu q. Integrate both sides and divide by mu: y = (1 / mu) times (integral of mu q dx + C). The constant C rides along inside, multiplied by 1 / mu.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Solve y' + 2 y = 0. Here p = 2, so mu = e^(2 x). Then (e^(2 x) y)' = 0, giving e^(2 x) y = C and y = C e^(-2 x). Solve y' + y = e^x. Here mu = e^x, so (e^x y)' = e^x times e^x = e^(2 x). Integrate: e^x y = (1/2) e^(2 x) + C, hence y = (1/2) e^x + C e^(-x). Variable coefficient: y' + (1/x) y = 1 for x > 0. Then mu = e^(integral of (1/x) dx) = e^(ln x) = x, so (x y)' = x. Integrate: x y = x^2 / 2 + C, giving y = x/2 + C/x.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In y' - 3 y = 6, what is the integrating factor? 2) Solve y' + y = 0 with y(0) = 4. 3) Solve y' - y = e^x (careful, the guess overlaps). 4) What is mu for y' + (2/x) y = x? 5) Solve 2 y' + 4 y = 0. Answers: 1) mu = e^(-3 x). 2) y = 4 e^(-x). 3) mu = e^(-x), so (e^(-x) y)' = 1, giving e^(-x) y = x + C and y = (x + C) e^x. 4) mu = e^(2 ln x) = x^2. 5) divide first: y' + 2 y = 0, so y = C e^(-2 x).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: computing mu before dividing through so the coefficient of y' is 1. Mistake: dropping the +C, or forgetting that it too gets divided by mu. Exit: (a) What is the integrating factor for y' + p(x) y = q(x)? (b) After multiplying by mu, what does the left side always become? Answers: mu = e^(integral of p dx); the derivative (mu y)'.

questions.prompt: The order of the equation y'' + 3 y' + 2 y = x is…
questions.explanation: The highest derivative present is y'', so the equation is second order.

questions.prompt: Separating dy/dx = x y and integrating gives the general solution…
questions.explanation: dy/y = x dx integrates to ln|y| = x^2/2 + C, so y = A e^(x^2/2).

questions.prompt: For the linear equation y' + 2 y = e^x, the integrating factor is…
questions.explanation: With p = 2, mu = e^(integral of 2 dx) = e^(2 x).

questions.prompt: Which constant solution is hidden when you separate dy/dx = y (1 - y) by dividing?
questions.explanation: Dividing by y(1 - y) assumes it is nonzero, so y = 0 and y = 1 must be added back.

questions.prompt: Solving dy/dx = y^2 with y(0) = 1 gives…
questions.explanation: Separating gives -1/y = x + C; the condition forces C = -1, so y = 1/(1 - x).

questions.prompt: Before finding the integrating factor of 3 y' + 6 y = 9, you should first…
options: divide through so y' has coefficient 1
questions.explanation: Standard form needs the coefficient of y' to be 1: y' + 2 y = 3.

lessons.title: Modeling with first-order equations: growth, cooling, mixing
lessons.grammar_note: In a rate model, dy/dt equals rate in minus rate out — get the signs of those two flows right and the equation writes itself.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Translate three classic situations — populations, temperature, and tanks of brine — into first-order equations and solve them. Warm-up: if a quantity grows at a rate proportional to how much is present, what equation are you looking at?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Exponential growth and decay come from dy/dt = k y, whose solution is y = y0 e^(k t); with k < 0 it decays, and the half-life (the time to halve) is ln(2) / |k|. Newton's law of cooling says a body approaches its surroundings at a rate proportional to the gap: dT/dt = -k (T - T_env), giving T = T_env + (T0 - T_env) e^(-k t). Mixing problems track the amount S(t) of dissolved substance in a tank: dS/dt = (rate in) - (rate out), where rate in is the inflow concentration times the inflow speed, and rate out is the outflow speed times the current concentration S / V. When inflow and outflow speeds match, the volume V stays constant and the equation is linear.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Decay: a sample obeys dy/dt = -0.2 y with y0 = 100. Then y = 100 e^(-0.2 t), and its half-life is ln(2) / 0.2, about 3.47 time units. Cooling: coffee at 90 degrees in a 20-degree room with k = 0.1 satisfies T = 20 + 70 e^(-0.1 t); after 10 units T is about 20 + 70 e^(-1) = 45.7 degrees. Mixing: a 100-liter tank of pure water gets brine at 2 grams/liter flowing in at 5 liters/min, well stirred, draining at 5 liters/min. Then dS/dt = (2)(5) - 5 (S/100) = 10 - S/20. This is linear; its steady state is S = 200 grams, the amount at which inflow and outflow of salt balance.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Write the equation for a population growing at 3 percent per year in continuous time. 2) A 80-degree object cools in a 20-degree room; what is T_env? 3) In the tank above, what is dS/dt when S = 100? 4) If y = y0 e^(k t) has half-life 5, what is k? 5) What steady-state salt amount does dS/dt = 10 - S/20 approach? Answers: 1) dP/dt = 0.03 P. 2) T_env = 20 degrees. 3) 10 - 100/20 = 10 - 5 = 5 grams/min. 4) k = -ln(2)/5, about -0.139. 5) set dS/dt = 0: S = 200 grams.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: dropping the minus sign in cooling, which would make the object heat up forever. Mistake: using concentration where the model tracks total amount (or the reverse) in a mixing tank. Exit: (a) What is the half-life for dy/dt = k y? (b) In a mixing tank, what two flows make up dS/dt? Answers: ln(2) / |k|; rate in minus rate out.

lessons.title: Second-order linear homogeneous equations (constant coefficients)
lessons.grammar_note: For a y'' + b y' + c y = 0 the roots of a r^2 + b r + c = 0 decide everything — real and distinct, real and repeated, or complex.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write the characteristic equation of a constant-coefficient second-order equation and read off the general solution in all three root cases. Warm-up: what are the roots of r^2 - 5 r + 6 = 0?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For a y'' + b y' + c y = 0, try y = e^(r t). Substituting turns the equation into the characteristic (auxiliary) equation a r^2 + b r + c = 0. Three cases follow from its roots. Distinct real roots r1 and r2 give y = C1 e^(r1 t) + C2 e^(r2 t). A repeated real root r (when the discriminant is zero) gives y = (C1 + C2 t) e^(r t) — the extra factor of t supplies the needed second independent solution. Complex roots r = alpha plus or minus beta i give oscillation inside an exponential envelope: y = e^(alpha t) (C1 cos(beta t) + C2 sin(beta t)). Two arbitrary constants appear because the equation is second order.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Distinct real: y'' - 5 y' + 6 y = 0 has r^2 - 5 r + 6 = 0, roots r = 2 and r = 3, so y = C1 e^(2 t) + C2 e^(3 t). Repeated: y'' - 4 y' + 4 y = 0 has r^2 - 4 r + 4 = (r - 2)^2 = 0, a double root r = 2, so y = (C1 + C2 t) e^(2 t). Complex: y'' + 4 y = 0 has r^2 + 4 = 0, so r = plus or minus 2 i, giving alpha = 0 and beta = 2, hence y = C1 cos(2 t) + C2 sin(2 t). With damping, y'' + 2 y' + 5 y = 0 has r = -1 plus or minus 2 i, so y = e^(-t) (C1 cos(2 t) + C2 sin(2 t)).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Solve y'' - y = 0. 2) Solve y'' + 6 y' + 9 y = 0. 3) Solve y'' + 9 y = 0. 4) Solve y'' - 3 y' + 2 y = 0. 5) What is the general solution when the characteristic roots are -2 plus or minus 3 i? Answers: 1) roots 1 and -1, so y = C1 e^t + C2 e^(-t). 2) (r + 3)^2 = 0, double root -3, so y = (C1 + C2 t) e^(-3 t). 3) roots plus or minus 3 i, so y = C1 cos(3 t) + C2 sin(3 t). 4) roots 1 and 2, so y = C1 e^t + C2 e^(2 t). 5) y = e^(-2 t) (C1 cos(3 t) + C2 sin(3 t)).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the extra factor of t for a repeated root, which leaves you one solution short. Mistake: mishandling complex roots — the real part becomes the exponential envelope and the imaginary part becomes the cosine/sine frequency. Exit: (a) What is the general solution for a double root r? (b) For roots alpha plus or minus beta i, what plays the role of the oscillation frequency? Answers: (C1 + C2 t) e^(r t); beta.

lessons.title: Second-order nonhomogeneous equations (undetermined coefficients)
lessons.grammar_note: The full solution is y = y_h + y_p: the homogeneous solution plus one particular solution of the forced equation.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Solve a y'' + b y' + c y = g(t) by finding the homogeneous solution, guessing a particular solution matched to g, and combining them. Warm-up: what does the general solution of a nonhomogeneous linear equation add together?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For a y'' + b y' + c y = g(t), the general solution is y = y_h + y_p. Here y_h is the general solution of the homogeneous equation (set g to 0), and y_p is any single solution of the full equation. The method of undetermined coefficients guesses y_p from the shape of g: if g is a polynomial, guess a polynomial of the same degree; if g is A e^(r t), guess a constant times e^(r t); if g is a sine or cosine of frequency w, guess a cos(w t) + b sin(w t). Substitute the guess, match coefficients, and solve for them. Key exception: if your guess already solves the homogeneous equation, multiply it by t (or t^2 for a double root) so it becomes independent.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Constant forcing: y'' - 3 y' + 2 y = 4. The homogeneous roots are 1 and 2, so y_h = C1 e^t + C2 e^(2 t). Guess y_p = A (a constant): then 2 A = 4, so A = 2 and y = C1 e^t + C2 e^(2 t) + 2. Exponential forcing: y'' - y = e^(2 t). Guess y_p = A e^(2 t): then 4 A - A = 1, so A = 1/3 and y_p = (1/3) e^(2 t). Overlap case: y'' - 3 y' + 2 y = e^t. Since e^t already solves the homogeneous equation, guess y_p = A t e^t instead; substituting gives A = -1, so y_p = -t e^t.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What form should y_p take for g(t) = 5 t + 1? 2) Find y_p for y'' - y = 3. 3) Find A in y_p = A e^(3 t) for y'' - y = e^(3 t). 4) Why must you multiply the guess by t in y'' + y = cos(t)? 5) Write the full solution of y'' - 3 y' + 2 y = 4. Answers: 1) a first-degree polynomial, y_p = a t + b. 2) guess constant A: -A = 3, so y_p = -3. 3) 9 A - A = 1, so A = 1/8. 4) because cos(t) already solves y'' + y = 0, so the plain guess would give zero. 5) y = C1 e^t + C2 e^(2 t) + 2.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting only y_p and forgetting to add y_h, which loses the arbitrary constants. Mistake: not multiplying by t when the guess overlaps a homogeneous solution (this is the seed of resonance). Exit: (a) What two pieces make up the full solution? (b) What do you do when your guess already solves the homogeneous equation? Answers: y_h plus y_p; multiply the guess by t (or t^2).

questions.prompt: The characteristic equation of y'' - 4 y' + 4 y = 0 has…
questions.explanation: (r - 2)^2 = 0 gives the double root r = 2, so y = (C1 + C2 t) e^(2 t).

questions.prompt: The general solution of y'' + 9 y = 0 is…
options: C1 cos(3 t) + C2 sin(3 t)
questions.explanation: The roots are plus or minus 3 i, so the solution oscillates as C1 cos(3 t) + C2 sin(3 t).

questions.prompt: In a mixing tank with inflow and outflow both 5 liters/min, the volume V…
questions.explanation: Equal inflow and outflow keep the volume fixed, which keeps the equation linear.

questions.prompt: For the full solution of a y'' + b y' + c y = g(t), y equals…
questions.explanation: You add the homogeneous solution and one particular solution: y = y_h + y_p.

questions.prompt: Newton's law of cooling dT/dt = -k (T - T_env) drives the temperature toward…
questions.explanation: The gap decays exponentially, so T approaches T_env as time grows.

questions.prompt: If a particular-solution guess already solves the homogeneous equation, you should…
questions.explanation: Multiplying by t (or t^2 for a double root) makes the guess independent of y_h.

lessons.title: Mechanical and electrical oscillations, and resonance
lessons.grammar_note: A mass-spring-damper m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t) and an RLC circuit L q'' + R q' + (1/C) q = E(t) are the same equation wearing different labels.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Set up the mass-spring-damper equation, name its damping regimes, connect it to the RLC circuit, and explain resonance. Warm-up: for x'' + 4 x = 0, what is the natural frequency?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A mass on a spring with damping obeys m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t): mass times acceleration equals the spring force -k x, the damping force -c x', and any external forcing F(t). With no damping or forcing, x'' + (k/m) x = 0 oscillates at the natural angular frequency omega0 = sqrt(k/m). Damping c splits the behavior by the discriminant of the characteristic equation: overdamped (two real roots, no oscillation), critically damped (a repeated root, fastest non-oscillating return), and underdamped (complex roots, oscillation that decays inside an e^(alpha t) envelope). The electrical twin is the RLC circuit L q'' + R q' + (1/C) q = E(t), where inductance acts like mass, resistance like damping, and 1/C like the spring constant. Resonance occurs when a periodic force pushes near omega0: the response amplitude grows large, and in the undamped ideal case it grows without bound like t.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Undamped: x'' + 4 x = 0 gives omega0 = sqrt(4) = 2, so the motion is x = C1 cos(2 t) + C2 sin(2 t) with period 2 pi / 2 = pi. Underdamped: x'' + 2 x' + 5 x = 0 has roots -1 plus or minus 2 i, so x = e^(-t)(C1 cos(2 t) + C2 sin(2 t)) — it rings but dies out. Critically damped: x'' + 4 x' + 4 x = 0 has the double root -2, so x = (C1 + C2 t) e^(-2 t), returning to rest without overshoot. Pure resonance: x'' + omega0^2 x = cos(omega0 t) forces at the natural frequency, and because cos(omega0 t) solves the homogeneous equation the particular solution carries a factor of t, x_p = t sin(omega0 t) / (2 omega0), whose amplitude grows over time.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) For x'' + 9 x = 0, what is omega0? 2) Which damping regime has a repeated characteristic root? 3) In the RLC analogy, what plays the role of the spring constant k? 4) Does an underdamped system oscillate? 5) Near what frequency does a lightly damped system show resonance? Answers: 1) omega0 = 3. 2) critically damped. 3) 1/C, the reciprocal of the capacitance. 4) yes, with an amplitude that decays exponentially. 5) near its natural frequency omega0.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading the natural frequency as k/m instead of sqrt(k/m). Mistake: expecting oscillation in the overdamped or critically damped cases — only underdamped systems ring. Exit: (a) What is the natural angular frequency of m x'' + k x = 0? (b) Resonance is strongest when forcing frequency is near what value? Answers: sqrt(k/m); the natural frequency omega0.

lessons.title: Laplace transforms
lessons.grammar_note: The Laplace transform turns calculus into algebra: derivatives in t become multiplication by s, with the initial values folded in.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Apply a small table of Laplace transforms and the derivative rule to convert an initial value problem into an algebra problem, then invert to recover the solution. Warm-up: what should happen to a derivative y' after you take its transform?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Laplace transform of f(t) is F(s) = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-s t) f(t) dt, which trades a function of time for a function of s. A short table covers most needs: L of 1 is 1/s; L of e^(a t) is 1/(s - a); L of t is 1/s^2; L of sin(b t) is b/(s^2 + b^2); L of cos(b t) is s/(s^2 + b^2). The reason it solves ODEs is the derivative rule: L of y' is s Y - y(0), and L of y'' is s^2 Y - s y(0) - y'(0), where Y is the transform of y. Applying the transform to a linear equation with constant coefficients turns it into a linear algebra equation for Y. Solve for Y, break it into simple pieces with partial fractions, and read each piece back off the table (the inverse transform).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: First order: y' + y = 0 with y(0) = 2. Transform: (s Y - 2) + Y = 0, so (s + 1) Y = 2 and Y = 2/(s + 1). Inverting gives y = 2 e^(-t). Second order: y'' + y = 0 with y(0) = 0 and y'(0) = 1. Transform: (s^2 Y - s times 0 - 1) + Y = 0, so (s^2 + 1) Y = 1 and Y = 1/(s^2 + 1), which inverts to y = sin(t). Forced first order: y' - y = 1 with y(0) = 0. Transform: (s Y - 0) - Y = 1/s, so (s - 1) Y = 1/s and Y = 1/(s(s - 1)). Partial fractions: 1/(s(s - 1)) = -1/s + 1/(s - 1), which inverts to y = -1 + e^t.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is L of e^(3 t)? 2) What is L of cos(2 t)? 3) Write L of y'' in terms of Y, y(0), y'(0). 4) Transform y' + 3 y = 0 with y(0) = 5 and solve for Y. 5) Invert Y = 1/(s^2 + 9). Answers: 1) 1/(s - 3). 2) s/(s^2 + 4). 3) s^2 Y - s y(0) - y'(0). 4) (s + 3) Y = 5, so Y = 5/(s + 3) and y = 5 e^(-3 t). 5) y = (1/3) sin(3 t), since L of sin(3 t) is 3/(s^2 + 9).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the initial-value terms in the derivative rule, which quietly drops the initial conditions. Mistake: stopping at Y and never taking the inverse transform back to y(t). Exit: (a) What is L of y' in terms of Y and y(0)? (b) What table entry has transform 1/(s - a)? Answers: s Y - y(0); e^(a t).

lessons.title: Systems of ODEs and Euler's method
lessons.grammar_note: Any nth-order equation becomes a first-order system by naming the lower derivatives as new variables.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Rewrite a higher-order equation as a first-order system and approximate a solution numerically with Euler's method. Warm-up: if you let v = y', what first-order equation does y satisfy?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A single higher-order equation can be recast as a system of first-order equations by naming each lower derivative. For y'' = f(t, y, y'), set v = y'; then y' = v and v' = f(t, y, v) — two coupled first-order equations. A linear system such as x' = a x + b y, y' = c x + d y can be written in matrix form and studied through the eigenvalues of that matrix. When no formula is available, Euler's method steps forward numerically: choose a step size h, and from y_(n+1) = y_n + h times f(t_n, y_n) march from the initial point. Smaller h generally means a more accurate approximation, because Euler follows the tangent line over each step and the error shrinks as the steps get shorter.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Convert y'' + y = 0 to a system: let v = y'; then y' = v and v' = -y. Euler on dy/dt = y with y(0) = 1 and h = 0.1: y1 = 1 + 0.1 times 1 = 1.1; y2 = 1.1 + 0.1 times 1.1 = 1.21; y3 = 1.21 + 0.1 times 1.21 = 1.331. After two steps the estimate at t = 0.2 is 1.21, while the true value e^(0.2) is about 1.2214 — close, and closer still if h shrinks. Convert y'' - 3 y' + 2 y = 0: with v = y', the system is y' = v and v' = 3 v - 2 y.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Rewrite y'' = -4 y as a first-order system. 2) In Euler's method, what is the update formula? 3) Do one Euler step for dy/dt = 2 y, y(0) = 3, h = 0.5. 4) Does halving h usually raise or lower the error? 5) Rewrite y'' + y' + y = 0 as a system. Answers: 1) let v = y'; then y' = v and v' = -4 y. 2) y_(n+1) = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n). 3) y1 = 3 + 0.5 times (2 times 3) = 3 + 3 = 6. 4) it lowers the error. 5) let v = y'; then y' = v and v' = -v - y.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting Euler's method to be exact — it accumulates error over many steps. Mistake: forgetting to introduce a new variable for each derivative below the top when building a system. Exit: (a) What substitution turns y'' = f into a first-order system? (b) What is the Euler update formula? Answers: set v = y' (and higher derivatives as needed); y_(n+1) = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n).

questions.prompt: The order of a differential equation is…
options: the power on the highest derivative
the number of constants in g(t)
questions.explanation: Order is the highest derivative present; degree would be the power on it.

questions.prompt: A constant solution of an autonomous equation dy/dt = f(y) occurs exactly where…
questions.explanation: Where f(y) = 0 the rate of change is zero, so y stays put — an equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Separating dy/dx = -x / y leads to which family of curves?
questions.explanation: y dy = -x dx integrates to x^2 + y^2 = constant, a family of circles.

questions.prompt: The integrating factor for y' + (1/x) y = 1 (with x > 0) is…
questions.explanation: mu = e^(integral of (1/x) dx) = e^(ln x) = x, so (x y)' = x.

questions.prompt: For dy/dt = k y, the half-life of the quantity is…
questions.explanation: Setting e^(k t) = 1/2 gives t = ln 2 / |k|.

questions.prompt: The general solution of y'' - 5 y' + 6 y = 0 is…
options: C1 cos(6 t) + C2 sin(6 t)
questions.explanation: The characteristic roots are 2 and 3, giving C1 e^(2 t) + C2 e^(3 t).

questions.prompt: A repeated characteristic root r = 2 gives the general solution…
options: C1 cos(2 t) + C2 sin(2 t)
questions.explanation: A double root needs the extra factor of t: (C1 + C2 t) e^(2 t).

questions.prompt: To solve y'' - 3 y' + 2 y = 4, a good particular-solution guess is…
questions.explanation: Constant forcing calls for a constant guess; here 2 A = 4, so y_p = 2.

questions.prompt: Undamped resonance, forcing x'' + omega0^2 x = cos(omega0 t), produces a response whose amplitude…
questions.explanation: Because the forcing matches a homogeneous solution, the particular solution carries a factor of t and grows over time.

questions.prompt: Using Laplace transforms, L of y'' equals…
questions.explanation: The second-derivative rule folds in both initial values: s^2 Y - s y(0) - y'(0).

questions.prompt: Euler's method advances the solution by the rule…
questions.explanation: Each step follows the tangent: y_(n+1) = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n).

questions.prompt: Rewriting y'' + y = 0 as a first-order system with v = y' gives…
questions.explanation: From v = y' and y'' = -y, the system is y' = v and v' = -y.
